newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan analysts wary on financial sector reforms.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan analysts wary on financial sector reforms.

text.p: Pakistani analysts reacted warily on Tuesday to a reform plan for the state-run financial sector unveiled by the caretaker government.
They said the plan, spelled out to Pakistani reporters on Monday by economic adviser Shahid Javed Burki, would have to be implemented properly if it was to succeed.

If the plan was carried out successfully, it should lead to a greater degree of efficiency and slash the mounting bad debts of state-run banks and financial institutions and help the process of privatisation.
"These are all proposed plans. We just have to wait and see how much of it is going to be implemented," Naunman Sheikh, senior analyst at KASB & Co, told Reuters.

Burki was quoted by newspapers on Tuesday as saying the caretaker government, appointed earlier this month after the sacking of Benazir Bhutto's government, has approved a comprehensive reform programme for the state-run financial sector.
He was quoted as saying all bad debts of the state-run banks and institutions would be acquired by a temporary body called the Resolution Trust Corporation which would pursue payment.

The State (central) Bank of Pakistan's annual report for fiscal 1995/96 (July-June) reported total debts of state-owned banks and financial institutions at 113.2 billion rupees in June 1996, compared with 101 billion rupees in the year-ago period.
Burki said the recovery drive would be helped by stricter foreclosure laws and special banking tribunals and courts.
Sheikh said the foreclosure law would allow banks to confiscate property and other assets of defaulters before going to court for settlement or rescheduling of the loan.
"This will certainly help in discouraging wilful defaulters, who in the past have been defaulting on their dues and it was for the banks to approach courts for settlement," Sheikh said.
But Kalim Aziz, head of research at ING Baring Securities, said implementation of such strict laws would be difficult.
"Most of the defaulters are those who carry political clout. It will remain to be seen if any action is taken against such people," Aziz said.
Burki said the government had also approved the merger or restructuring of some financial institutions before offering them for privatisation.
Aziz said unless the plans were followed up by privatisation of the institutions, the bad debts problem would return.
Burki said some bad debts may be marketed as long-term government securities or ten-year maturity bonds so that some of the burden could be shared.
Aziz said the plan for transfer and legal status of such bonds was not clear, but such schemes had been helpful in handling debt problems in Latin America.
Sheikh said restructuring the state-owned financial sector through speeding up privatisation or merging them into a few larger institutions should be taken as a positive signal.
Analysts agreed with Burki that the institutions have been abused in the past, carry enormous bad debts and that the problem had to be dealt with very quickly.
Aziz said the state-owned banks and institutions were serving no purpose and were being abused for political lending and were a burden on government expenses.
